family_judgments.evidence: The four interaction types are recognizably distinct practice formats and each preserves a coherent offer-making purpose.
Changing the names from Maya to Alex does not materially vary the recurring open-window scenario or the identical target response across all four items.

criteria.evidence: The instruction names the required words and the visible sentence ending tells learners where their response belongs.
Typing a short phrase before “the window?” is a coherent constrained-cloze interaction.
The situation and vocabulary are concrete and familiar, including “cold,” “window,” and “help”.
Alex offering to close an open window for someone who is cold is natural.
The supplied words and fixed object provide an appropriate level of support for B2 practice.
The response expectation is specific and the short answer is straightforward to score.
The dialogue identifies Alex as the speaker and asks for an offer phrased as a question.
The labelled incomplete turn clearly supports a short-text continuation by Alex.
“Getting cold,” “because,” and “open” are accessible everyday language for B2 learners.
The proposed offer is an appropriate response after identifying the open window as the cause of the cold room.
The dialogue supplies enough pragmatic support while asking learners to produce a complete short question.
This is a standard, compact dialogue-completion interaction with a clear expected response.
The instruction, stem, and context consistently ask for Alex’s appropriate offer.
The labelled alternatives and single-choice mode match the task wording.
The options use the same basic, familiar vocabulary throughout.
The cold-room situation makes the intended offer easy to interpret pragmatically.
The item tests selection among clearly contrasting question forms without difficult vocabulary.
The interface needs only a standard radio-button selection and has one clear answer.
The context identifies Alex as the speaker, while the cue explicitly gives the words required for the first-person offer.
A full-sentence text response is appropriate for rewriting the supplied statement as a direct offer.
The source sentence and cue use common vocabulary with no specialist terms.
A direct offer to close the window follows naturally from Maya feeling cold.
The task requires a controlled perspective shift from Alex’s reported action to Alex’s direct speech, which is plausible at B2.
The cue and expected full sentence are sufficiently explicit for ordinary typed-response delivery and scoring.

summary: This is a clear, deployable set of standard practice formats, but it offers little within-family variety beyond format changes.
